questions.q: What does Credential Guard actually do with NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets?
options: It encrypts them with a user-chosen password and stores them in the registry
It isolates them inside a separate, hypervisor-protected process (LSAIso.exe) using Virtualization-Based Security, outside normal lsass.exe memory
It deletes them immediately after each logon so nothing is ever cached
It moves them to a cloud service for safekeeping
questions.explain: Credential Guard uses VBS to run an isolated LSAIso.exe process; the real secrets never live in lsass.exe's own memory space, so an attacker with kernel access can't simply read them out.

questions.q: Which of these is a real hardware/configuration requirement for Credential Guard?
options: A 64-bit CPU with virtualization extensions and SLAT, plus UEFI with Secure Boot enabled
No hardware requirements exist at all — it runs on any configuration
Windows 10/11 Home edition specifically
A 32-bit CPU with no virtualization support
questions.explain: Credential Guard depends on VBS, which requires virtualization extensions, SLAT, and UEFI Secure Boot, and is only available on Enterprise/Education or Server editions.

questions.q: What does LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) specifically change about lsass.exe?
options: It runs lsass.exe as a Protected Process Light, so only signed, trusted code can load into its address space
It requires a TPM 2.0 chip to function at all
It disables lsass.exe entirely so no authentication can occur
It moves lsass.exe's memory into a separate hypervisor-protected container
questions.explain: RunAsPPL hardens lsass.exe itself against code injection by making it a Protected Process Light — a different mechanism than Credential Guard's VBS isolation.

questions.q: What does setting RunAsPPL to a value of 2 do, instead of 1?
options: Permanently disables LSA Protection
Doubles the protection level with no logging
Has no effect — only 0 and 1 are valid values
Runs LSA Protection in audit mode, logging what would be blocked (Event IDs 3065/3066) without enforcing it yet
questions.explain: A value of 2 is the audit-mode equivalent to Lesson 14's ASR audit rollout — it logs what would be blocked so incompatible drivers or plugins can be found before full enforcement.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why does a Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords attempt fail on a host with both Credential Guard and LSA Protection enabled?
options: Credential Guard means there's nothing to dump since secrets never live in lsass.exe's memory, and LSA Protection blocks the module injection Mimikatz needs in the first place
Mimikatz is incompatible with all versions of Windows regardless of configuration
Both controls simply delete Mimikatz's executable file before it can run
Only one of the two controls actually does anything; the other has no real effect
questions.explain: The two controls stop two different steps of the same attack technique: isolation removes what there is to steal, and process hardening blocks the injection needed to even attempt the theft.
